title: Binary Search — From Trace Table to Working Code
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: How does a linear search differ from a binary search?
questions.answer: Linear search checks sequentially; binary search repeatedly halves the remaining sorted range.
options: There is not enough information to determine the result.
Linear search checks sequentially; binary search repeatedly halves the remaining sorted range.
Linear search checks sequentially; binary search repeatedly halves the remaining unsorted range.
questions.feedback: Model answer: Linear search checks sequentially; binary search repeatedly halves the remaining sorted range.

questions.prompt: Why can binary search miss a target that exists in an unsorted array?
questions.answer: Because comparisons rely on sorted order to discard one half safely.
options: Because comparisons rely on unsorted order to discard one half safely.
There is not enough information to determine the result.
Because comparisons rely on sorted order to discard one half safely.
questions.feedback: Model answer: Because comparisons rely on sorted order to discard one half safely.

blocks.title: Key vocabulary
items: sorted array — Values arranged in order, so comparisons can eliminate ranges.
target — The value the algorithm is trying to locate.
midpoint — The middle index of the current candidate range.
lower bound — The first index still under consideration.
upper bound — The last index still under consideration.
iteration — One execution of the loop body.

blocks.title: Start with valid bounds
blocks.text: The last index is 7, not 8. Array length is not a valid index.

blocks.title: Find the midpoint
blocks.text: Integer division gives index 3. Compare its value (18) with target (31).

blocks.title: Discard half
blocks.text: All positions through index 3 are too small. Keep only 4–7.

blocks.title: Stop when found or exhausted
blocks.text: If low becomes greater than high, return -1. Never assume the target exists.

blocks.title: Worked example · Write a function that returns the target’s index
blocks.text: Your task: Create BinarySearch , a C# function that takes a sorted integer array and a target integer . It must return the array index (position) where the target is found, or -1 when the target is absent. int[] numbers = {3, 7, 12, 18, 24, 31, 45, 60}; Syntax: int = integer · [] = array · numbers = name · { } = values. Question: The array holds 8 values. Why is the final index 7 ? Example: Search for 31 → return 5 (its index, not its value). Search for 13 → return -1 (not found).
